title: Our Mutual Friend: A Literary Discussion

segments.title: Opening: The Dust and the Gentleman

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked — a close, unhurried look at what many consider the greatest of Dickens's novels.
Our Mutual Friend was published in monthly parts between 1864 and 1865 — the last completed novel Dickens would write.
It is a novel about money — about what money does to people, what people do for money, and who gets buried under the weight of it all.
It opens on a river, with a body being fished from the Thames — and it never quite leaves that dark water.
Joining me today are three extraordinary readers who bring very different lenses to this remarkable book.
Oliver Trevelyan has narrated more classic novels on audio than perhaps anyone alive.
He comes to Dickens as a performer first — hearing the rhythms, the comic timing, the voices that were always written to be heard rather than simply read.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don — a traditionalist who reads novels as moral investigations of character under pressure.
He will keep us honest about what the novel is actually doing with its people — as opposed to what we might wish it were doing.
And Dr Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who reads every novel as an anatomy of class and power.
In a novel built on dust heaps and inheritance and the labour of the forgotten, his perspective is — I'd argue — indispensable.
We begin today with the novel's strange foundations — its dust, its money, and the question of what goodness looks like in a world built on filth.
The first thing to say about Our Mutual Friend is that it starts like a Gothic nightmare and then somehow becomes one of the funniest books in the English language.
Those two things coexist — the rot and the laughter — and Dickens never apologises for either.
What I hear, performing this novel, is a writer who is absolutely in command of register — who can switch from the mordant to the farcical within a single paragraph.
And then, just when you're enjoying the comedy, he drops a sentence on you that feels like the floor giving way.
What strikes me, returning to this novel after many years, is how persistently Dickens insists that goodness is real — not a social construct, not a performance, but a force.
He locates it, characteristically, not in the educated or the refined, but in people like the Boffins — people society has used hard and paid little.
And he makes a quite extraordinary claim about that goodness — that it cannot ultimately be suppressed, even by the worst circumstances.
I want to begin with exactly the passage Edmund is gesturing at, because I think it contains one of the most remarkable sentences in the whole novel.
Dickens is describing the Boffins — these two people whom their former master had wrung dry of work for as little money as he could pay.

He describes their master as — and this is the text — 'the hard wrathful and sordid nature that had wrung as much work out of them as could be got in their best days, for as little money as could be paid.'
'For as little money as could be paid to hurry on their worst.'
That is a description of exploitation — precise, unflinching, and delivered without any softening.
And then he writes this — listen to it —
'For, Evil often stops short at itself and dies with the doer of it; but Good, never.'
That is not a sentimental claim — it is a theological one, and Dickens means every word of it.
When you read that sentence aloud — and I have read it aloud, many times — it lands like a tolling bell.
The rhythm does the work: 'Evil often stops short at itself and dies with the doer of it' — that's a long clause, winding down, stopping.
And then: 'but Good, never.' — two words and a comma.
The comma does something extraordinary — it makes you pause inside the word 'never,' as if to feel its full weight before it lands.
What Oliver has identified is precisely what distinguishes Dickens from the merely clever satirists of his age.
He can frame a moral law — 'this is the eternal law,' he actually says — without for a moment losing the particularity of these two specific human beings.
The Boffins are not emblems of virtue — they are people, with ten thousand weaknesses and absurdities, as the text carefully tells us.
The moral law works through imperfect, ordinary people — that is the novel's great insistence.
I agree — and I'd add that this novel is also perfectly capable of puncturing its own moral grandeur with savage comedy.
There's a passage I love — the scene with the stuffed specimens in Wegg's lair, those grotesque taxidermic witnesses.
Dickens uses them to deliver a verdict on Wegg's jealousy and treachery — but the verdict is delivered by an alligator.
The text says the alligator's smile might be invested with the meaning —
'All about this was quite familiar knowledge down in the depths of the slime, ages ago.'
The slime is history itself — ancient, amoral, patient.
And every betrayal and every act of greed is already in there, logged, unremarkable.
And then there is Miss Jenny Wren — who is, I would argue, the most original comic creation in the whole novel.
She has a moment — after Fledgeby has been thoroughly beaten — where she contemplates the plasters being applied to his wounds.
And she says — with that silent laugh of hers —
'I think the young man's tricks and manners make a claim upon his friends for a little pepper?'
The question mark does the whole job — it's the most polite form of gleeful revenge in Victorian fiction.
She's not angry — she's delighted.
Dust heaps, alligators, and a doll's dressmaker seasoning a villain's wounds — we are firmly in the world of Our Mutual Friend.
In the next segment, we'll look more closely at the Thames — the river that opens this novel and never quite lets it go.

segments.title: Money's Corruption: Following the Golden Thread

utterances.text: Welcome back to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked.
We've been circling the great dust-heap of Dickens's final completed novel — the money, the mud, the marvellous cast of the living and the self-consciously dead.
Today we turn to what might be the novel's most intricate moral mechanism: the way inherited wealth poisons identity before it can even be claimed.
With me, as always, are three extraordinary readers of this novel.
Oliver Trevelyan — actor, writer, and the man whose voice has guided more readers through the classics than perhaps anyone alive.
Oliver hears the novel as a performer first — the rhythms, the comic timing, the moments Dickens wrote specifically for the voice.
Sir Edmund Leigh — retired Oxford don, whose conviction that great fiction is above all a story about individual moral character has sharpened over a lifetime of close reading.
Edmund reads Our Mutual Friend as a test of souls — not a pamphlet about economics.
And Dr. Daniel Rosen — cultural historian, who insists that the novel's portrait of money is never merely symbolic but is a precise anatomy of how class power actually operates.
Daniel finds the novel's radicalness in the places Dickens himself may not have fully intended.
The passages before us today all concern John Harmon — or Rokesmith, as we know him for most of the book — and the extraordinary deception he constructs around himself and Bella Wilfer.
Oliver, let's begin with you — because this is a man who stages his own death as a kind of audition for his future wife.
The audition — yes, that's exactly the right word, and I suspect Dickens would have approved of it.
Because what Harmon does — lying in that public-house bed, having very nearly been murdered and drowned — is something utterly theatrical.
He decides to exploit his own near-death as a plot device.
Listen to how Dickens puts it — and he's very precise here:
'the thought entered my head of turning the danger I had passed through, to the account of being for some time supposed to have disappeared mysteriously, and of proving Bella.'
'Proving Bella.' As if she's a theorem.
And the sentence is brilliant because it's half confession, half theatrical programme note — 'the danger I had passed through, to the account of.'
He's converting near-murder into dramatic capital.
I think what strikes me in that passage is something rather more morally serious than theatrical ingenuity.
Harmon explicitly names what he fears: perpetuating the fate of his father's riches — that they should lead to nothing but evil.
That phrase — 'the fate that seemed to have fallen on my father's riches' — is the moral hinge of the entire novel.
Dickens is not diagnosing capitalism, as some would have it.
He is exploring what a man of conscience does when the inheritance handed to him has already corrupted everyone who touched it.
That is a question of character — individual, interior, irreducibly personal.
Edmund, I respect the distinction, but I think the novel itself refuses it.
Look at what Dickens actually gives us in the chapter that follows — and this is Harmon reconstructing the logic of his own deception.
He doesn't begin with individual conscience — he begins with a system:
'the distrust engendered by his wretched childhood and the action for evil — never yet for good within his knowledge then — of his father and his father's wealth on all within their influence.'
'All within their influence.' This isn't one man's private failing.
The wealth acts on everyone it touches — it is structural, not personal.
Harmon's 'moral timidity,' as Dickens calls it, is the product of that system, not a flaw in his character that he must overcome by individual willpower.
And what's so extraordinary as a performer — reading that passage aloud — is the accumulative quality Dickens builds into the syntax itself.
He even flags it: 'as many a man lapses into many a condition, without perceiving the accumulative power of its separate circumstances.'
The sentence is doing what it describes — each clause adding weight to the last until the whole thing is almost too heavy to lift.
And then you arrive at this brilliant trap Harmon finds himself in:
'Was it for him to have the shame of buying her, or the meanness of punishing her?'
Both horns of the dilemma are contemptible — and Dickens gives equal moral weight to each.
That's the novel's cruelty and its genius: there is no clean exit from money's gravity.
Oliver's right to press on that dilemma — and I'd note it's a dilemma only because Harmon has a moral imagination at all.
A lesser man — a Wegg, say — would simply have taken the money and congratulated himself.
Now, the scheme itself — getting common sailors' clothes, drifting into Bella Wilfer's orbit — is also where I think Dickens is at his most novelistically daring.
The passage describing the plot with Radfoot is fascinatingly provisional:
'the plot was made out of our getting common sailors' dresses, and throwing ourselves in Bella Wilfer's neighbourhood, and trying to put ourselves in her way.'
'Throwing ourselves in her neighbourhood' — this is not a scheming villain's plan; it is almost embarrassingly tentative.
A man hoping to be judged fairly, not to manipulate — which rather vindicates him, in my reading.
I'm not sure 'tentative' exonerates the plan, Edmund.
Harmon's scheme still treats Bella as an object to be evaluated — a specimen in a test he has designed entirely without her consent.
The class dimension matters too: he dresses as a common sailor to observe a woman who is herself economically powerless.
What the novel does brilliantly — and this is where Dickens earns his radicalism — is show Bella becoming aware of exactly this power imbalance, from the inside.
There's a moment when she's with Lizzie Hexam — a woman who has given up everything for love without prospect of return — and Bella's self-awareness breaks through.
Dickens renders it as comedy — but it is devastating comedy:
'There, you little mercenary wretch! Do you hear that? Ain't you ashamed of yourself?'
She's addressing herself — and then she literally pokes herself in the side as penance.
That self-accusation is the real arc of the novel: not the inheritance plot, but the internal reckoning with what money has made her want to be.
And the voice Dickens gives her in that moment — 'Ain't you ashamed of yourself' — it's cockney self-reproach delivered at speed.
It's the voice of the London street turned inward as conscience.
And this connects, I think, to the passage with Betty Higden — which is one of the quietest, most affecting moments in these chapters.
Rokesmith watches from a doorway — and Dickens's language is suddenly very still:

'The Secretary looked on from a doorway at the boofer lady thus encircled, and still looked on at the boofer lady standing alone there, when the determined old figure with its steady bright eyes was trudging through the streets, away from paralysis and pauperism.'
'Away from paralysis and pauperism.' That's Betty Higden's entire story compressed into four words.
And Rokesmith — who is watching all of it — is still 'the Secretary.' Dickens won't let him step out from behind his disguise even in the narration.
That is beautifully observed, Oliver.
The identity question runs through every sentence — Harmon cannot be seen clearly because he cannot see himself clearly while the money remains unclaimed.
And yet — before we grow too solemn about the corruption wrought by great wealth — Dickens also gives us Mr. Boffin on the subject of charity.
Which is, I have to say, one of the finest comic passages in the novel — and one of the most accurate observations about institutional philanthropy ever committed to English prose.
Boffin, who has just become very rich, is bewildered by the begging letters pouring in — and by the preposterous hierarchies they invoke:

'Patrons and Patronesses, and Vice-Patrons and Vice-Patronesses, and Deceased Patrons and Deceased Patronesses, and Ex-Vice-Patrons and Ex-Vice-Patronesses, what does it all mean in the books of the Charities that come pouring in on Rokesmith as he sits among 'em pretty well up to his neck!'
The escalating absurdity of those titles — 'Ex-Vice-Patrons' — Dickens is simply cataloguing the thing into self-parody.
What I value in Boffin is that his indignation is moral, not political — he is offended by the impudence of it, not by the system that produces it.
Edmund, I'll take Boffin's indignation — but I can't let the system off the hook quite so easily.
The comedy of those charity titles is a precise satire on how philanthropy launders class privilege.
'If Mr Tom Noakes gives his five shillings ain't he a Patron?' — Dickens is showing us that the charitable gift is really a purchase: you are buying a title, buying social legitimacy.
The same logic that makes Bella mercenary is at work in the Patronesses and Ex-Vice-Patrons — money converting everything into status.
And Rokesmith is literally buried under it — 'sitting among 'em pretty well up to his neck.'
A man whose identity is submerged, surrounded by the documents of false generosity.
The golden thread runs through all of it — identity, inheritance, the performance of virtue, the impossibility of clean hands when money is involved.

What strikes me is how Dickens holds the comedy and the tragedy in the same hand — Boffin raging about Patronesses in the same world where Betty Higden trudges away from pauperism with steady bright eyes.
In our next segment, we'll follow the money further downstream — to the river itself, and to what Dickens does with those who work in its mud and its margins.

segments.title: Laughter in the Mire: Dickens's Comic Voice

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, the podcast that takes Dickens's last completed novel seriously — and joyfully.
I'm your host, and today we have three extraordinary guests around the table.
Oliver Trevelyan — actor, writer, and the voice behind more classic audiobooks than anyone living — brings the ear of a performer to everything Dickens wrote.
Sir Edmund Leigh, retired Oxford don and one of the most exacting readers of the Victorian novel, who believes character and moral imagination are the heart of any great fiction.
And Dr Daniel Rosen, cultural historian, who reads every novel as an anatomy of class power — and finds in Dickens a more radical writer than Dickens perhaps knew himself.
Today's segment is about Dickens's comic voice — the laughter that runs through the mire of this novel like a dark, irrepressible current.
Oliver, you've spent more time inside Dickens's prose rhythms than almost anyone alive.
Where does the comedy of Our Mutual Friend sit for you — and what makes it different?
The comedy in this novel has grit under its fingernails.
It's not the warm, rolling comedy of Pickwick or the festive comedy of Christmas — it's sharper, it's meaner, and it knows exactly what it's doing.
Take Silas Wegg — one of Dickens's great grotesques, a man with a wooden leg and the moral architecture of a cockroach.
The scene where he lays out his extortion scheme to Mr Venus is a masterclass in comic pomposity.
Dickens gives him this absurd rhetorical architecture — every clause beginning with 'That,' like a man reading a legal document he's written himself with trembling pride.
And then comes the glorious centrepiece of the whole plan — the price, reduced to a single word.
'He considered it plain that such price was stateable in a single expressive word, and that the word was, Halves!'
The exclamation mark is doing real work there — it's Wegg's own inner fanfare.
What strikes me about Wegg is that the comedy doesn't diminish the villainy — it intensifies it.
Dickens understood something that is sometimes overlooked: that small men with large ambitions are genuinely dangerous, not merely ridiculous.
The language of the passage — 'abject moral bondage and slavery' — is grotesquely overblown, yet Wegg means every syllable.
'He should be kept in a state of abject moral bondage and slavery until the time when they should see fit to permit him to purchase his freedom at the price of half his possessions.'
There is something almost Swiftian in that sentence — the language of tyranny deployed by a man who sells ballads from a street corner.
Dickens is laughing, yes — but he is also showing us the precise grammar of petty oppression.
Edmund is right to identify the grammar of it — because what Wegg is doing structurally is mimicking the language of legitimate property ownership.
He calls Boffin 'the minion of fortune and the worm of the hour' — that phrase is doing real ideological work.
It inverts the moral hierarchy so that Wegg becomes the rightful claimant and Boffin the usurper.
What Dickens is satirising is not simply Wegg's greed — it's the ease with which any claim to property can be dressed up in the language of justice.
The comedy is ruthless because the target is real.
And Dickens knows exactly when to pay it all off — which is in one of the great physical comedy scenes of the whole novel.
Wegg has been scheming and posturing across hundreds of pages — and then Sloppy picks him up.
Like a sack of flour.
And then — and this is Dickens at his most gleeful — Sloppy spots a scavenger's cart at the corner.
'Mr S. found it impossible to resist the temptation of shooting Mr Silas Wegg into the cart's contents. A somewhat difficult feat, achieved with great dexterity, and with a prodigious splash.'
'A prodigious splash.' Three words, and the whole comic arc of Silas Wegg is complete.
He came from the dust, he schemed over the dust, and the dust — or something very like it — reclaims him.
There is a rightness to that ending that is almost classical — hubris met with a kind of divine comedy.
And it is prepared for, beautifully, just a few pages earlier, when the Secretary warns Wegg off with a single, magnificent line.
'Be careful what insolent liberties you take in that gentleman's presence, or I will throw you after it.'
It's the kind of line that an actor can do almost nothing wrong with — the sentence already contains its own timing.
Dickens had an absolute instinct for the line that lands without needing any assistance from the performer.
I'd agree with that, Edmund, and add — as a performer — that the threat is funny precisely because it is absolutely sincere.
There's no winking at the audience. He will throw him after it.
And that's what separates great comic writing from merely clever writing — the comedy lives inside the character's total conviction.
I want to hold both those things together for a moment — the comedy and the violence — because I think this novel insists we do.
Charley Hexam's confrontation with Headstone is another place where the laughter is entirely absent — and the accusation is clinical, precise, brutal.
Dickens gives Charley this extraordinary list of grievances, all of them perfectly logical from the point of view of a boy trying to climb out of his class.
Listen to how he frames his injury — not as moral outrage, but as reputational damage:
'You know that I took you with me to his chambers in the Temple when I told him my opinion of him, and made myself responsible for my opinion of you.'
There's no comedy there — but the absence of comedy is itself a kind of diagnosis.
Charley has learned to value himself in the currency the system has given him, and that is the saddest joke of all.
And then there's Mrs Sprodgkin — who gives us a completely different register of Dickensian comedy.
Not satirical anatomy, not physical farce — but a portrait of benign, indestructible absurdity.
The narrator's description of her church behaviour is a small masterpiece:

'She was a member of the Reverend Frank's congregation, and made a point of distinguishing herself in that body, by conspicuously weeping at everything, however cheering, said by the Reverend Frank in his public ministration.'
'However cheering' — those two words contain an entire character study.
She isn't moved despite the cheering; she weeps because of it, through some magnificent private logic only she can follow.
What I find remarkable about that passage is the warmth beneath the satire.
The Milveys are not caricatures of Christian virtue — they are genuinely good people, gently exasperated, who nonetheless 'made the best of her, as they did of all their troubles.'
Dickens had a sentimental streak — I would not deny it — but here the sentiment is earned by the comedy that surrounds it.
Mrs Sprodgkin is ridiculous; the Milveys' patience with her is admirable; and both things are held in the same light, without contradiction.
I'll grant you that the Milveys are genuinely sympathetic — Dickens means us to admire them.
But Mrs Sprodgkin herself is interesting precisely because her absurdity has a social dimension — she lodges her complaints, as Dickens puts it, as if applying for a warrant before a magistrate.
She has translated her emotional and spiritual needs into the language of grievance and legal procedure — which is the only language available to her.
Dickens laughs at that, affectionately — but the joke contains the diagnosis.
So across all these scenes — Wegg's extortion speech, Sloppy's magnificent delivery, Mrs Sprodgkin's ecclesiastical grievances — we see a comic voice that is never just entertaining.
It diagnoses, it anatomises, and — as Oliver says — it always knows when to pay off.
In our next segment, we'll be turning to the river — the novel's great dark artery — and what it means that so much of this story begins and ends in the water.

segments.title: Secrets Buried: The Architecture of Concealment

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, the programme that takes Dickens's last completed novel apart passage by passage to see how it works.
I'm your host, and today we're exploring one of the most architecturally complex chapters in the book — the great unmasking in which John Harmon finally steps out of the shadows.
Three brilliant minds join me around the table.
Oliver Trevelyan has narrated more classic novels than anyone alive, and he hears Dickens the way a conductor hears a score — for rhythm, timing, and the precise moment when the comedy turns grave.
Sir Edmund Leigh is the retired Oxford don who insists that great fiction is finally about individual character under moral pressure — and he will not let us forget it.
And Dr Daniel Rosen reads every novel as an anatomy of class power — who owns what, who controls whom, and what the law actually protects.
Our focus today is Harmon's confrontation with Silas Wegg — the revelation of the Dutch bottle, the buried will, and the elaborate trap that was set for a blackmailer.
Oliver, you've read this chapter aloud — what hits you first as a performer?
What hits me first is the sheer controlled violence of Harmon's voice — and I mean that literally, because Dickens keeps pulling the physical action right into the speech.
He doesn't just announce that the will is worthless — he shakes the man, rattles the paper in his face, and threatens to knock his brains out, all in the same breath.
And then there is that extraordinary parenthetical — the one that stops the legal declaration dead in its tracks.

'It is a will of my late father's, of more recent date than the will proved by Mr Boffin (address whom again, as you have addressed him already, and I'll knock you down), leaving the whole of his property to the Crown.'
That parenthesis — tucked inside a solemn legal sentence — is a masterpiece of comic timing and genuine menace simultaneously.
No other novelist alive in 1865 would dare put a physical threat inside the grammar of a legal document, and make it land as both funny and frightening.
As a performer, you have to hold both registers at once — and Dickens gives you the roadmap in the punctuation itself.
Oliver is right about the parenthesis, and I don't wish to quarrel with his theatrical reading of it.
But what strikes me as the moral centre of this scene is something altogether more sober — the figure of Boffin.
Harmon tells us that when Boffin found this later will — the will that gave him everything absolutely and reviled John and his dead sister by name — it distressed him beyond measure.

'That Dutch bottle distressed him beyond measure, because, though I and my sister were both no more, it cast a slur upon our memory which he knew we had done nothing in our miserable youth, to deserve.'
There is the moral imagination of the novel in a single sentence.
Boffin gains a fortune, and his first instinct is to mourn what it cost the dead — children whom he could not protect, whose names are dragged through an old miser's spite.
That is not a social programme at work — that is goodness, plain and irreducible.
I don't dispute Boffin's goodness, Edmund — but I want to press on what makes that goodness necessary in the first place.
What Dickens shows us here is that property law is so rigid, so indifferent to human feeling, that even a man of genuine decency is afraid to destroy a document that he knows is morally poisonous.
He buries it in the Mound instead — the great heap of dust that is already the novel's image of accumulated, undifferentiated wealth.
The law doesn't protect the living or the dead — it protects the document.
And Harmon himself names this with a kind of bitter precision — the paper, he says, is worth less than the rotten cork of the Dutch bottle.
'The paper now rattling in your hand as I shake you — and I should like to shake the life out of you — is worth less than the rotten cork of the Dutch bottle, do you understand?'
That rattling paper — it's a magnificent image — is what the system of inheritance produces: documents that outlive their human meaning and keep damaging people long after everyone involved is dead.
What I can't get over, listening to Daniel lay that out, is how Dickens manages to make the violence in this scene feel like justice rather than brutality.
Because Harmon is genuinely roughing Wegg up — this isn't metaphorical.
He says, and Dickens writes this with what I can only call joyful candour,
'I mean to knock your head against the wall — and I'd give a thousand pounds for leave to knock your brains out.'
And yet we cheer him on, don't we?

Because Wegg is so comprehensively vile, and Dickens has been so patient in building the case against him, that when the reckoning comes, even the knocking of a head against a wall feels morally earned.
That is a very difficult trick to pull off — and it requires the entire preceding novel.
Oliver's point about earned reckoning is well taken, and it brings me to what I think is the most revealing element of this whole episode: the deliberate prolonging of Wegg's delusion.
Harmon confesses quite openly that they allowed Wegg to go on believing he held power, precisely in order to make his disappointment heavier when it came.
He says as much:

'I tell you this, that you may know we knew enough of you to persuade Mr Boffin to let us lead you on, deluded, to the last possible moment, in order that your disappointment might be the heaviest possible disappointment.'
Now — one might ask whether this is entirely chivalrous on Harmon's part.
But I think Dickens is making a precise moral distinction: between mercy, which Wegg has forfeited, and justice, which the innocent dead are owed.
Wegg spent years plotting the ruin of a good man — the calibration of his punishment seems to me quite appropriate.
Edmund's distinction between mercy and justice is useful, but I want to pull at a thread he's left dangling: the role of surveillance in all of this.
Harmon doesn't just outwit Wegg — he and Sloppy have been watching him systematically, shadow-like, for an extended period.
Listen to how Dickens phrases this — it's almost institutional in its precision.
'Sloppy has long made it the chief occupation and delight of his life, to attend you like your shadow.'
The language of occupation and delight — it's almost playful, but the function it describes is a private intelligence operation run by the wealthy against a would-be usurper.
Property, in this novel, protects itself — and it enlists the loyal poor to do so.
Sloppy is devoted to Boffin, yes — but his devotion is also his labour, his function, the role the system finds for him.
Daniel, that reading is bracing — and I half accept it.

But I confess I find something genuinely touching in the image of Sloppy trailing Wegg through the Mound day after day, this great lumbering loyal creature with his ear pressed to the keyhole of a schemer's soul.
Dickens understood that fidelity — even inarticulate, untheorised fidelity — is one of the most powerful things a human being can offer.
And the fact that Sloppy delights in it — that word, delight — suggests Dickens won't let us reduce it to mere function.
What strikes me, pulling these threads together, is how completely the architecture of concealment in this chapter works on every level at once.
The buried bottle, the buried will, the buried identity — Harmon himself is the longest-running secret in the novel, and this chapter is where all those buried things surface together.
You've each illuminated a different stratum of that — the comic violence, the moral weight, the machinery of property and surveillance.
We'll continue in the next section with what Harmon's unmasking costs him — and what he finds on the other side.

segments.title: The Refuse Heap Speaks: Class, Worth, and Waste

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, the programme where we take one of Dickens's grandest, most labyrinthine novels and open it up — chapter by chapter, layer by layer.
Today's segment goes to the heart of the novel's obsession: what money does to people, and what people do in the presence of money.
We're looking at Nicodemus Boffin — the Golden Dustman — newly rich, installed in his aristocratic mansion, and immediately besieged by every variety of human want and human greed.
With me today are three voices I trust absolutely to make sense of all this.
Oliver Trevelyan — actor, writer, and the man whose voice has given life to more classic novels than anyone alive — brings us the performer's ear for Dickens's comic genius.
Sir Edmund Leigh — retired Oxford don and one of the finest close readers of Victorian fiction — reads these passages as moral tests for individual character.
And Dr. Daniel Rosen — cultural historian and our sharpest analyst of class power — will show us what the dust heap reveals about how wealth really circulates in Victorian England.
Let's begin with the mansion itself — that extraordinary simile Dickens gives us for Boffin's new life.
You know the moment that made me laugh out loud the first time I read this — truly laugh, not smile, not chuckle — is that cheese.
Because Dickens doesn't reach for grandeur when he wants to puncture aristocratic pretension.
He reaches for a cheese.
The passage describes Boffin feeling that his mansion was, and I must read this properly —
"like an eminently aristocratic family cheese, it was much too large for his wants, and bred an infinite amount of parasites."
The eminently aristocratic family cheese — I mean, that is a joke constructed with the precision of a Swiss watchmaker.
And then the parasites — because of course a big cheese breeds mould, and a big fortune breeds exactly the same thing.
Dickens is doing at least three things at once and making it look effortless.
Oliver is quite right that the comedy is executed with extraordinary craft.
But I think what's happening beneath the surface of that joke is a rather serious observation about Boffin's character.
Boffin does not pretend the mansion suits him.
He knows it's too large; he knows it breeds parasites.
And he accepts it — this is the phrase that arrests me — as a sort of perpetual Legacy Duty.
That is a man who is not corrupted by wealth — not yet — because he sees it clearly for what it is.
He has the fundamental decency to be a little embarrassed by his own fortune.
I want to hold onto that word — parasites — because Dickens uses it precisely, and it changes what the passage is doing.
The parasites bred by aristocratic wealth are not simply freeloaders on an individual.
They are the entire social apparatus — charities, institutions, the nobility itself — that exists to extract value from whoever has accumulated it.
And what Dickens shows us in the passages about Boffin's correspondence is how systematic that extraction is.
The letters don't arrive by chance — they are an organised machinery for redistributing wealth upward, dressed in the language of benevolence.
And that machinery is catalogued with ferocious energy in the letters Boffin's secretary has to process.
Oliver, this is very much your territory — Dickens at full comic velocity.
Oh, it's glorious — this is Dickens conducting at full orchestra.
The passage cataloguing the charity letters — I've performed this at literary evenings and it never fails.
Fifty-seven churches to be erected with half-crowns, forty-two parsonage houses to be repaired with shillings — the accumulation is almost musical.
But then he gives us a single specimen letter — and this is where the timing becomes quite magnificent.
"Large fat private double letter, sealed with ducal coronet."
Six words of description — and you can see it, you can feel the weight of it in your hand.
And then the letter itself: utterly pompous, thoroughly flattering, signed by a Duke — and ending with a postscript that the steward's fee is three guineas.
Dickens calls it 'friendly' and 'thoughtful in the postscript' — that deadpan is worth a hundred exclamation marks.
What strikes me about that letter is the particular viciousness of the lithograph detail.
The Duke's letter is printed by the hundred — Nicodemus Boffin's name filled in by a different hand altogether.
So the flattery is itself a mass-produced commodity — the personal appeal utterly impersonal.
This is not merely comic — it is a precise observation about how reputation functions as currency.
Boffin is not being approached as a human being but as a source — a marked man, as the narrator puts it.
Edmund has identified something crucial — the phrase Dickens uses is 'the man marked by a stroke of notoriety.'
Boffin has not changed — his character, his decency, is intact — but the mark of wealth has been placed on him.
And that mark is what every predatory institution in Victorian England is trained to see.
The narrator asks: 'Oh the varieties of dust for ocular use, offered in exchange for the gold dust of the Golden Dustman!'
Every appeal is itself a kind of refuse — moral rubbish dressed up as philanthropy.
The dust heap generates wealth, and then wealth generates a new kind of dust — the waste product of social performance.
And if the corporate beggars — the charities and the dukes — are one species, Dickens gives us an entire taxonomy of the individual beggars too.
Edmund, that catalogue of individual supplicants — I wonder if you find it as darkly comic as Oliver does, or if something else is happening there?
I think it is one of the most uncomfortable passages in the novel, and that discomfort is deliberate.
Dickens skewers the fraudulent beggars — the inspired ones with their angelic whispers, the independent ones who want only a loan at five per cent — with real relish.
But then there are those who are simply desperate — the daughters of officers, the men and women who have documents, as he wryly puts it.
He writes that they call their scraps documents, but they are —
"as to papers deserving the name, what minced veal is to a calf."
The comedy there is sharp, even cruel — but it does not entirely discharge our concern for these people.
Dickens is not letting us simply laugh and move on.
I absolutely agree — and the beggars who threaten to be 'cold in death' at a quarter to one on Tuesday is where I feel the novel change key.
The precision of that — a quarter to one — makes it grotesque, but it also makes it oddly sad.
Someone sat down and wrote that.
And what the passage does — which I think is Dickens at his most extraordinary — is hold comedy and tragedy in the same sentence without one destroying the other.
The minced veal simile makes you laugh, and then you think — wait, that person needed something, and they got nothing.
What I want to press on is that word 'documents' — because Dickens has chosen it with surgical care.
To have documents is to have standing — legal, social, institutional standing.
These people are trying to perform legitimacy because they have no other resources.
Their scraps of paper are a claim to personhood in a system that has refused to recognise them.
And Dickens — brilliantly, heartlessly — reduces those claims to minced veal.
He is reporting on a system that has already done that reduction — he's not initiating it.
And hovering over all of this is the question of what wealth actually amounts to — which Wegg's discovery about John Harmon's will makes rather startling.
Daniel, Wegg reads out a will that essentially says Boffin gets the little mound — and the Crown gets everything else.
This is one of the most quietly devastating moments in the novel, and it's delivered in the most grotesque possible way — through Wegg.
Wegg reads out the will's key passage with his characteristic buoyancy —

"Inasmuch as he has never made friends, and has ever had a rebellious family, he, John Harmon, gives to Nicodemus Boffin the Little Mound, which is quite enough for him, and gives the whole rest and residue of his property to the Crown."
'Quite enough for him' — those three words contain the entire misanthropy of old John Harmon.
The man who built the dust heap — who accumulated everything — dies having made no friends and leaving it to the state.
Wealth, in this novel, cannot be passed on cleanly — it is always contaminated by the conditions of its accumulation.
I read that will differently — and I think the difference matters.
What Dickens is showing us in old Harmon is the consequence of a life lived without love — without the moral bonds that give wealth any meaning.
The rebellious family, the absence of friends — these are not symptoms of a system.
They are the harvest of a particular character — a man who chose money over human connection at every turn.
Boffin getting the Little Mound is not an irony about wealth — it is a moral judgment about who deserves what.
What I keep coming back to is that Wegg reads this with 'blandness and buoyancy' — as the text says.
He is delighted — because he thinks this will give him power over Boffin.
And here is where Dickens performs a kind of moral judo — the man who thinks he holds power is in fact the most pitiful figure in the room.
Because what does Wegg actually do with his power?
He stands outside Boffin's house at night, brooding over it.
Dickens calls it being the house's 'Evil Genius' — and I promise you, that phrase is both menacing and completely absurd.
The Wegg passage about power is one I return to constantly, because Dickens is making an argument there that is almost aphoristic.
The narrator states it directly —
"Power — unless it be the power of intellect or virtue — has ever the greatest attraction for the lowest natures."
That is Dickens operating in a register very close to political philosophy.
Wegg's corruption is not personal — it is the inevitable product of what power does to a man who has nothing else.
The system that produced his poverty also shaped the particular appetites that poverty leaves behind.
I'll grant Daniel that the passage is damning — but I resist reducing Wegg to a product of circumstance.
Dickens specifies: the power of intellect or virtue is excepted.
The implication is that a nature capable of those things would not be degraded by power in the same way.
Wegg chooses to hover outside a house in the dark, feeding his own fantasy of destruction.
That is not circumstance — that is character.
And perhaps what's most unsettling is that Wegg's fantasy — stripping the roof off Boffin's house like a house of cards — is itself a kind of image from the dust heap.
Everything in this novel — the letters, the wills, the hovering menace — circles back to the question of what value is, and who gets to decide.
We'll return after the break to look at how Dickens maps this same territory through the novel's river — and what flows through it besides water.

segments.title: Performance and Persona: Reading Dickens's Unreliable Depths

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, the programme that takes Dickens's last completed novel apart — scene by scene, chapter by chapter — to find out what makes it tick.
Today's segment concerns performance and persona — the question of how Dickens uses surface and depth, comedy and concealment, to construct characters who are never quite what they seem.
With me, as ever, are three remarkable voices on this novel.
Oliver Trevelyan has recorded more classic novels for audio than almost anyone living, and he comes to Dickens as a performer first — someone who hears the comic timing encoded in every sentence.
Sir Edmund Leigh brings the perspective of a lifetime's Oxford scholarship — a reader who believes the moral imagination is where the real action lies, not the social programme.
And Dr. Daniel Rosen reads every institution in a Dickens novel as a mechanism of power — philanthropy, money, charity, all of it anatomised with clear-eyed precision.
Oliver, let's begin with you — because what strikes me about Our Mutual Friend is how often Dickens uses physical comedy to set up something genuinely complicated.
Yes, and the Betty Higden sequence is the perfect place to start, because the comedy is almost scandalously good before anything serious is allowed to happen.
We have the orphan — this small, chubby, unnamed child — perched on a board across the doorway, overcome with excitement.
And Dickens describes what happens next with a kind of deadpan clinical precision that is absolutely devastating.
He writes — and I savour every syllable of this —
"Being an orphan of a chubby conformation, he then took to rolling, and had rolled into the gutter before they could come up."
"Of a chubby conformation" — as though his roundness were a geological fact, a natural law, something the inquest would have to record.
The verb 'took to rolling' is the masterstroke — it implies the orphan had, in some sense, found his vocation.
Oliver is quite right that the comedy is precise — but I'd ask us to notice what it's doing morally, not merely technically.
The scene conspires to place Rokesmith and Mrs Boffin in possession of this upside-down, purple-faced child at the very moment they are meeting a woman who needs to trust them.
Dickens calls it — with characteristic irony — "unlawful possession."
That phrase is doing considerable work: it invokes the language of the law, of custody, of property — in a scene ostensibly about charity and compassion.
Good intentions, Dickens reminds us here, arrive in the world looking awkward, purple-faced, and upside down.
And the board across the doorway — which Dickens notes acts as a trap for everybody equally — that's not incidental stage business.
The literal threshold that nobody can cross cleanly is the material condition of this encounter.
The Boffins' money wants to reach Betty Higden's poverty, and what stands between them is a structural obstacle that trips up everyone regardless of their goodwill.
The comedy and the critique are the same gesture.
I'll grant Daniel's reading — but I want to press on to something even more extraordinary in this same chapter, which is Betty Higden's description of Sloppy.
Because this is one of those moments where Dickens produces, in five words, an image so complete that every scholar of modernist literature should feel a slight chill.
Betty is explaining, with magnificent simplicity, that Sloppy reads the newspaper to her aloud.
"He do the Police in different voices."
That sentence will haunt T.S. Eliot so deeply he'll use a version of it as the working title for The Waste Land — but forget Eliot for a moment.
What Dickens has caught is the entire performance of reading: the social news rendered as theatre, as entertainment, as the one gift an illiterate woman's boy can give her.
Seven words, and the relationship between Sloppy and Betty Higden is fully alive.
The grammar of "he do" is doing something rather precise, and I think it's worth pausing on it.
Dickens writes Betty's dialect faithfully — not as a joke at her expense, but as the syntax of genuine pride.
"He do the Police in different voices" — said by a woman who cannot read herself — is a statement of devotion and wonder.
The novel here is not condescending to Betty Higden; it is paying her close, respectful attention.
That moral attentiveness — the refusal to caricature those at the bottom — is where Dickens's real greatness lives.
I agree entirely with Edmund on the respect shown to Betty Higden — but I want to connect it to something structural in the novel.
Sloppy's gift — performing the news in different voices — is a kind of labour.
It's the labour of interpretation, of giving the world's events a human shape, performed for someone the world has otherwise given nothing to.
In that household — poor, precarious, dependent on kindness — art and care are the same thing.
And the novel notices that.
Let's move forward in the novel, then, to the great revelation scene — the moment when Bella Wilfer finally sees through Mr Boffin's performed miserliness.
Oliver, this is a scene of extraordinary emotional and comic complexity — and it hinges entirely on the question of persona.
It's one of the finest scenes in the whole novel — and fiendishly difficult to read aloud, because the joy is almost unbearably infectious.
Bella has placed the baby in John's arms — she has arranged the scene with the instinct of a great theatrical director — and then she kneels beside Mr Boffin.
And what comes out of her is not a speech — it's a cascade, a torrent of the word "please."
Dickens writes — and this must be read at pace, with all the exultant ringing laugh he prescribes —
"Please I have found out something not yet mentioned. Please I don't believe you are a hard-hearted miser at all, and please I don't believe you ever for one single minute were!"
That repetition of "please" — six times in the passage — is a child's word, a supplicant's word, and Bella deploys it as an instrument of demolition.
She is not merely forgiving Boffin — she is retracting her own former self, clawing back every contemptuous thought she ever had about money and worth.
This is, for me, the moral centre of the novel — and it arrives through an act of performance recognised as performance.
Boffin has performed villainy — has acted the miser — in order to correct Bella's character.
And Bella has undergone a genuine transformation — not forced upon her from without, but arrived at by her own moral intelligence.
"I don't believe you ever for one single minute were" — there is real steel in that sentence, even dressed in all those pleases.
Bella is not sentimental here; she is lucid.
And lucidity, in Dickens, is always a form of courage.
I find myself more ambivalent here than either Oliver or Edmund — though I feel the scene's power entirely.
What troubles me is that the whole elaborate deception — Boffin's performance — was orchestrated by men, to educate a woman about the proper relationship between love and money.
Bella is given a genuine arc — Dickens is too good a novelist for her transformation to be hollow — but the arc was designed for her without her knowledge or consent.
When she cries "please I have found out something not yet mentioned" — she has, yes, found it out; but the thing to be found was placed there for her to find.
That's not quite the same as freedom.
Daniel's point is well-taken — but I'd note that Dickens himself stages the scene so that the baby is handed off first.
"John dear, you're a good nurse; will you please hold baby?" — it's Bella who arranges the stage.
She is the director here, even if she did not write the play.
Which brings us neatly to a character who is entirely without such grace — and who, when the performance ends, meets its consequences rather physically.
Oliver, let's close with Silas Wegg — and the moment John Harmon's patience expires.
Wegg has been the novel's great performed villain — all unction and sarcasm, a man of second-hand words and borrowed menace.
And the novel finally dispenses with him in the most satisfying physical terms imaginable.
Dickens sets up the moment with perfect economy — Wegg was "entering on some sarcastic retort" — and then the prose shifts registers entirely.
"He found himself gripped by the cravat; shaken until his teeth chattered; shoved back, staggering, into a corner of the room; and pinned there."
Four verbs in quick succession — gripped, shaken, shoved, pinned — each one a sentence of its own.
This is Dickens writing action the way a great editor cuts film — and it's enormously, guiltily funny.
There is a long tradition in comedy — going back at least to Jonson, if not to Aristophanes — of the impostor physically unmasked.
Wegg has built an entire performance — the literary man, the injured party, the rightful claimant — and Harmon dismantles it not with argument but with his hands.
"His teeth chattered" — that detail is the comic puncture of all Wegg's pretension.
The body, in the end, does not lie.
What strikes me about this scene is what it displaces.
Wegg's crime is blackmail — extracting value by threatening revelation.
He is a small, failed version of how power actually operates in this novel — through threat, through information, through the cravat rather than the contract.
And the novel's answer to him is to give Harmon stronger hands.
Which is satisfying — but it is a fantasy of individual justice, not a structural solution.
The system that produced Wegg is still entirely intact at the end of the scene.
And on that productive tension — between the pleasures of individual justice and the persistence of the system — we'll leave this segment.

What Dickens gives us, again and again, is performance as the medium through which character is both concealed and revealed — and occasionally grabbed by the cravat and shaken until something true falls out.
We'll be back shortly.

segments.title: Closing: Redemption's Price in a Mercenary World

utterances.text: We've spent this episode tracing the novel's anatomy of money — how it corrupts, how it tests, and occasionally, how it redeems.
I want to close by asking each of you: does Dickens believe redemption is genuinely possible in this mercenary world, or is it always purchased at too high a price?
Oliver, you've been our guide to the texture of the prose all evening — where do you land?
I keep returning to Bella — because Dickens makes us feel her confusion before he explains it, which is the mark of a writer working at full stretch.
There's that extraordinary moment when she sits alone in her room, having just absorbed Mr Boffin's mercenary philosophy, and she interrogates herself in the looking-glass.
Dickens gives her this perfectly pitched internal monologue — let me read it as it sits on the page, because performance is the only honest criticism here.

'What he said was very sensible, I am sure, and very true, I am sure. It is only what I often say to myself. Don't I like it then? No, I don't like it — and, though he is my liberal benefactor, I disparage him for it. Then pray, what do you mean by this, you inconsistent little Beast?'
That last word — Beast — directed at herself, in the mirror, with equal parts comedy and self-disgust.
Dickens is showing us moral conscience arriving not as solemn epiphany but as comic self-accusation.
That is, to my mind, redemption made utterly believable — because it's ridiculous and painfully true at the same time.
Oliver is quite right that the comedy is doing serious moral work — though I'd press a little further on what precedes that self-examination.
Before Bella retreats to her room, Dickens gives us one of those moments of gothic economy that he does better than almost any other novelist in the language.
Bella glances at Boffin — and Dickens renders the entire catastrophe of a man's character in a single image.
'A dark cloud of suspicion, covetousness, and conceit, overshadowing the once open face.'
The word 'once' carries the whole weight of lost innocence — with the most devastating economy.
Now, I would resist any reading that says this corruption is simply capitalism's doing.
What Dickens is examining is the ancient moral problem of how wealth reveals what was latent in a man all along.
The redemption on offer — for Bella, at least — is the capacity to see that clearly, and to refuse it in herself.
Edmund's reading is elegant, but I think it lets the novel off a hook it has deliberately impaled itself on.
If this were simply about individual moral character, Dickens would have no need of Lizzie Hexam — and yet Lizzie is the novel's most searching test of what redemption actually costs.
Lizzie confides to Bella about Eugene — the man she loves across an unbridgeable class divide — and what she says is devastating in its precision.
'I would not have the light of them taken out of my life, for anything my life can give me.'
She is holding onto the light of something she has already decided she cannot have.
That is not redemption freely given — that is what the novel's social structure permits a woman of her class: not union, but the memory of light.
Dickens gives Bella her comic self-reckoning in the mirror because Bella has options the system allows her.
Lizzie gets something more austere — the grace of having confided it, once, and then carrying it forward alone.
Daniel has hit on something I find almost unbearably moving about that passage — Lizzie says 'my mind changed' the moment Bella walks in.
She had no intention of parting with a single word of it — and then, in the presence of another person willing to receive it, everything opened.
That is Dickens saying — quietly, without fanfare — that connection is its own form of redemption, even when the object of love remains unattainable.
Not everything gets resolved. Not everything gets saved. But some things get witnessed — and the novel insists that matters.
I'll concede that point to Oliver with more than usual readiness.
The novel does believe in witness. It believes two people honestly attending to one another is already a moral act in a world largely devoted to performance and pretence.
And I think — though Daniel may resist this — that Bella's mirror scene and Lizzie's confession are asking the same question by different means.
Can you see yourself and another person clearly, without the distortion of money or class or vanity?
If you can — even momentarily — Dickens seems to say that is where the human good resides.
I don't resist it entirely — but I want to note what that clarity costs Lizzie, materially and socially, and that Dickens does not flinch from it.
She carries the light of Eugene's eyes in her life — and she has already decided it is all she will carry.
That is not a failure of the novel's moral imagination — it is the novel refusing to paper over the cost of living decently in an indecent system.
Redemption, in this novel, is real — but it is never cheap.
Redemption is real — but never cheap. I think that is as fine a summary of this novel's moral vision as we are likely to arrive at.
A dark cloud overshadowing the once open face. An inconsistent little Beast staring back from the looking-glass. A light you carry but refuse to extinguish.
These are the images Dickens leaves us with — and they reward exactly the kind of attention that Oliver, Edmund, and Daniel have brought this evening.
My warmest thanks to Oliver Trevelyan, Sir Edmund Leigh, and Dr. Daniel Rosen.
And to you, for listening to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked.

c9:p29.text:
These two ignorant and unpolished people had guided themselves so far on
      in their journey of life, by a religious sense of duty and desire to do
      right. Ten thousand weaknesses and absurdities might have been detected in
      the breasts of both; ten thousand vanities additional, possibly, in the
      breast of the woman. But the hard wrathful and sordid nature that had
      wrung as much work out of them as could be got in their best days, for as
      little money as could be paid to hurry on their worst, had never been so
      warped but that it knew their moral straightness and respected it. In its
      own despite, in a constant conflict with itself and them, it had done so.
      And this is the eternal law. For, Evil often stops short at itself and
      dies with the doer of it; but Good, never.
c9:p29.summary: Dickens reflects that the Boffins, though ignorant and unpolished, have been guided by genuine religious duty and moral righteousness that even hardened souls cannot entirely resist.
c9:p29.best_quote: For, Evil often stops short at itself and dies with the doer of it; but Good, never.

c30:p22.text:
‘I have checked the calculation often, and it must have been two nights
      that I lay recovering in that public-house. Let me see. Yes. I am sure it
      was while I lay in that bed there, that the thought entered my head of
      turning the danger I had passed through, to the account of being for some
      time supposed to have disappeared mysteriously, and of proving Bella. The
      dread of our being forced on one another, and perpetuating the fate that
      seemed to have fallen on my father’s riches—the fate that they
      should lead to nothing but evil—was strong upon the moral timidity
      that dates from my childhood with my poor sister.
c30:p22.summary: While recovering in the public-house, John Harmon decides to let himself remain dead for a time to prove Bella's character and avoid perpetuating his father's wealth's curse.
c30:p22.best_quote: the thought entered my head of turning the danger I had passed through, to the account of being for some time supposed to have disappeared mysteriously, and of proving Bella

c31:p1.text:
He went over it all again. He had lapsed into the condition in which he
      found himself, as many a man lapses into many a condition, without
      perceiving the accumulative power of its separate circumstances. When in
      the distrust engendered by his wretched childhood and the action for evil—never
      yet for good within his knowledge then—of his father and his
      father’s wealth on all within their influence, he conceived the idea of
      his first deception, it was meant to be harmless, it was to last but a few
      hours or days, it was to involve in it only the girl so capriciously
      forced upon him and upon whom he was so capriciously forced, and it was
      honestly meant well towards her. For, if he had found her unhappy in the
      prospect of that marriage (through her heart inclining to another man or
      for any other cause), he would seriously have said: ‘This is another of
      the old perverted uses of the misery-making money. I will let it go to my
      and my sister’s only protectors and friends.’ When the snare into which he
      fell so outstripped his first intention as that he found himself placarded
      by the police authorities upon the London walls for dead, he confusedly
      accepted the aid that fell upon him, without considering how firmly it
      must seem to fix the Boffins in their accession to the fortune. When he
      saw them, and knew them, and even from his vantage-ground of inspection
      could find no flaw in them, he asked himself, ‘And shall I come to life to
      dispossess such people as these?’ There was no good to set against the
      putting of them to that hard proof. He had heard from Bella’s own lips
      when he stood tapping at the door on that night of his taking the
      lodgings, that the marriage would have been on her part thoroughly
      mercenary. He had since tried her, in his own unknown person and supposed
      station, and she not only rejected his advances but resented them. Was it
      for him to have the shame of buying her, or the meanness of punishing her?
      Yet, by coming to life and accepting the condition of the inheritance, he
      must do the former; and by coming to life and rejecting it, he must do the
      latter.
c31:p1.summary: Rokesmith justifies his original deception as harmless, traces how it spiralled beyond his control, and wrestles with the impossible choice between disgracing Bella or deceiving the Boffins.
c31:p1.best_quote: When in the distrust engendered by his wretched childhood and the action for evil—never yet for good within his knowledge then—of his father and his father's wealth on all within their influence, he conceived the idea of his first deception, it was meant to be harmless, it was to last but a few hours or days.

‘However, a sociable word or two on these mistakes became an easy
      introduction between us, and the weather was hot, and he helped me to a
      cool cabin on deck alongside his own, and his first school had been at
      Brussels as mine had been, and he had learnt French as I had learnt it,
      and he had a little history of himself to relate—God only knows how
      much of it true, and how much of it false—that had its likeness to
      mine. I had been a seaman too. So we got to be confidential together, and
      the more easily yet, because he and every one on board had known by
      general rumour what I was making the voyage to England for. By such
      degrees and means, he came to the knowledge of my uneasiness of mind, and
      of its setting at that time in the direction of desiring to see and form
      some judgment of my allotted wife, before she could possibly know me for
      myself; also to try Mrs Boffin and give her a glad surprise. So the plot
      was made out of our getting common sailors’ dresses (as he was able to
      guide me about London), and throwing ourselves in Bella Wilfer’s
      neighbourhood, and trying to put ourselves in her way, and doing whatever
      chance might favour on the spot, and seeing what came of it. If nothing
      came of it, I should be no worse off, and there would merely be a short
      delay in my presenting myself to Lightwood. I have all these facts right?
      Yes. They are all accurately right.

      and Deceased Patrons and Deceased Patronesses, and Ex-Vice-Patrons and
      Ex-Vice-Patronesses, what does it all mean in the books of the Charities
      that come pouring in on Rokesmith as he sits among ’em pretty well up to
      his neck! If Mr Tom Noakes gives his five shillings ain’t he a Patron, and
      if Mrs Jack Styles gives her five shillings ain’t she a Patroness? What
      the deuce is it all about? If it ain’t stark staring impudence, what do
      you call it?’
c31:p109.summary: Mr Boffin delivers a scathing critique of the proliferation of patronage titles and the pretension of charity donors who expect public recognition for their contributions.

c40:p72.text:
On this head, Silas Wegg had much to say. Silas had to say That, he would
      beg to remind his comrade, brother, and partner, of the impressive
      passages they had read that evening; of the evident parallel in Mr
      Boffin’s mind between them and the late owner of the Bower, and the
      present circumstances of the Bower; of the bottle; and of the box. That,
      the fortunes of his brother and comrade, and of himself were evidently
      made, inasmuch as they had but to put their price upon this document, and
      get that price from the minion of fortune and the worm of the hour: who
      now appeared to be less of a minion and more of a worm than had been
      previously supposed. That, he considered it plain that such price was
      stateable in a single expressive word, and that the word was, ‘Halves!’
      That, the question then arose when ‘Halves!’ should be called. That, here
      he had a plan of action to recommend, with a conditional clause. That, the
      plan of action was that they should lie by with patience; that, they
      should allow the Mounds to be gradually levelled and cleared away, while
      retaining to themselves their present opportunity of watching the process—which
      would be, he conceived, to put the trouble and cost of daily digging and
      delving upon somebody else, while they might nightly turn such complete
      disturbance of the dust to the account of their own private investigations—and
      that, when the Mounds were gone, and they had worked those chances for
      their own joint benefit solely, they should then, and not before, explode
      on the minion and worm. But here came the conditional clause, and to this
      he entreated the special attention of his comrade, brother, and partner.
      It was not to be borne that the minion and worm should carry off any of
      that property which was now to be regarded as their own property. When he,
      Mr Wegg, had seen the minion surreptitiously making off with that bottle,
      and its precious contents unknown, he had looked upon him in the light of
      a mere robber, and, as such, would have despoiled him of his ill-gotten
      gain, but for the judicious interference of his comrade, brother, and
      partner. Therefore, the conditional clause he proposed was, that, if the
      minion should return in his late sneaking manner, and if, being closely
      watched, he should be found to possess himself of anything, no matter
      what, the sharp sword impending over his head should be instantly shown
      him, he should be strictly examined as to what he knew or suspected,
      should be severely handled by them his masters, and should be kept in a
      state of abject moral bondage and slavery until the time when they should
      see fit to permit him to purchase his freedom at the price of half his
      possessions. If, said Mr Wegg by way of peroration, he had erred in saying
      only ‘Halves!’ he trusted to his comrade, brother, and partner not to
      hesitate to set him right, and to reprove his weakness. It might be more
      according to the rights of things, to say Two-thirds; it might be more
      according to the rights of things, to say Three-fourths. On those points
      he was ever open to correction.
c40:p72.summary: Wegg proposes an elaborate scheme: let Boffin excavate the Mounds at his own expense while they observe, then when the work is done, threaten him with the earlier will and extort half his property. If Boffin is caught secretly removing anything, they will interrogate and enslave him morally until he pays for his freedom.

c64:p118.text:
The words were but out of his mouth when John Harmon lifted his finger,
      and Sloppy, who was now close to Wegg, backed to Wegg’s back, stooped,
      grasped his coat collar behind with both hands, and deftly swung him up
      like the sack of flour or coals before mentioned. A countenance of special
      discontent and amazement Mr Wegg exhibited in this position, with his
      buttons almost as prominently on view as Sloppy’s own, and with his wooden
      leg in a highly unaccommodating state. But, not for many seconds was his
      countenance visible in the room; for, Sloppy lightly trotted out with him
      and trotted down the staircase, Mr Venus attending to open the street
      door. Mr Sloppy’s instructions had been to deposit his burden in the road;
      but, a scavenger’s cart happening to stand unattended at the corner, with
      its little ladder planted against the wheel, Mr S. found it impossible to
      resist the temptation of shooting Mr Silas Wegg into the cart’s contents.
      A somewhat difficult feat, achieved with great dexterity, and with a
      prodigious splash.

c64:p63.text:
‘Be careful what insolent liberties you take in that gentleman’s
      presence,’ said the owner of the hand which had done this, ‘or I will
      throw you after it.’

c57:p80.text:
‘If you had any part—I don’t say what—in this attack,’ pursued
      the boy; ‘or if you know anything about it—I don’t say how much—or
      if you know who did it—I go no closer—you did an injury to me
      that’s never to be forgiven. You know that I took you with me to his
      chambers in the Temple when I told him my opinion of him, and made myself
      responsible for my opinion of you. You know that I took you with me when I
      was watching him with a view to recovering my sister and bringing her to
      her senses; you know that I have allowed myself to be mixed up with you,
      all through this business, in favouring your desire to marry my sister.
      And how do you know that, pursuing the ends of your own violent temper,
      you have not laid me open to suspicion? Is that your gratitude to me, Mr
      Headstone?’
